title: Longest Repeated Stretch
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Find the longest stretch of consecutive characters that occurs in s at least twice, at two different starting positions. The two occurrences may overlap.

Return that stretch. If several different stretches share the longest length, return any one of them. If no character repeats at all, return the empty string.

examples.why: "issi" starts at positions 1 and 4. The two copies share the middle "i", and overlapping is allowed.
"xyz" appears at the start and at the end. "xy" appears three times but is shorter.
Every letter appears once, so not even a single character repeats.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters

compare.check: (args, got, expected) => { const s = args[0]; if (typeof got !== 'string' || got.length !== expected.length) return false; if (got === '') return true; const i = s.indexOf(got); return i >= 0 && s.indexOf(got, i + 1) >= 0; }

hints: If some stretch of length L appears twice, what can you say about stretches of length L − 1?

Repeats are monotone in length: if one of length L repeats, so does one of every shorter length. So you can binary search on L, as long as you can answer "is there a repeat of length exactly L?" quickly.

Answer that check in O(n) with a rolling hash: slide a window of length L, update its hash in O(1) per step, and look for a hash already seen. On a hash match, compare the actual characters to rule out collisions.

explain.intuition:
There are two separate ideas. First, the answer length can be binary searched. If a stretch of length L occurs twice, then its first L − 1 characters also occur twice. So "is there a repeated stretch of length L" is true up to some length and false after it, which is exactly the shape binary search needs.

Second, checking one length must be fast. Comparing every pair of windows is quadratic. A rolling hash turns each window into a number, and moving the window one step updates that number in O(1): remove the leftmost character's contribution, shift, add the new character. Put the hashes in a hash map; a hash that is already there is a likely repeat. Hashes can collide, so on a match compare the two actual windows before trusting it. With O(log n) lengths to check and O(n) per check, the whole search is about O(n log n).
steps: Binary search L between 1 and n − 1, remembering the start of the last repeat found.
To test a length L: compute the hash of s[0..L−1] and pow = base^L mod M.
Slide the window right one step at a time, updating the hash. Keep a map from hash to the window starts with that hash.
When the current hash is already in the map, compare the windows character by character. A real match means length L repeats: record its start and search longer; if no window matches, search shorter.
Return the substring for the longest length that matched, or "".
pitfalls: Trusting a hash match without comparing the strings. With 30 000 windows and a modulus around 10⁹, a collision in some check is quite likely.
Overflowing the hash in JavaScript. h * base must stay below 2⁵³, so keep the modulus near 10⁹ and the base small, or use BigInt.
Requiring the two occurrences not to overlap. In "aaaa" the answer is "aaa", from positions 0 and 1.

solutions.title: Every length, longest first, with a set
solutions.idea: Try lengths from n − 1 down; for each, put every window into a set and stop at the first window already seen.

solutions.title: Binary search on length + rolling hash
solutions.idea: Repeats of length L imply repeats of every shorter length, so binary search L. Each check slides a polynomial hash and verifies candidate matches.
